note.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant’s surface. Most water vapour leaves through stomata. Guard cells open or close the stomata by changing their turgor, and factors such as temperature, wind and humidity affect how quickly water is lost.
examples: On a windy day, moving air carries away humid air around leaves, so more water can evaporate.
When guard cells take in potassium ions, water enters them by osmosis and the stoma opens.
note.checkAnswer: Wind carries away humid air around the leaves, allowing more water to evaporate.
note.simple: Plants lose water vapour, mostly through tiny openings in their leaves. Wind usually speeds up this loss; high humidity slows it down.

note.title: Transpiration and stomata
steps: Water moves from the xylem into the cell walls of mesophyll cells.
Water evaporates from the moist walls into the air spaces in the leaf.
Water vapours move towards the stomata and pass to the outside air.
During daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells, water follows by osmosis, and the guard cells become turgid so the stoma opens.
In the evening, potassium ions and water move out of guard cells; they lose turgor and the stoma closes.
note.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapours from the plant surface. It occurs through stomata, the cuticle and lenticels.

written.text: How is the transpirational pull important in plants?
written.finalAnswer: Transpiration creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem tissue of leaves, stem and root. This pull is responsible for the transport of water and salts from root to leaves.

written.text: Transpiration is the loss of water from plants. Is it a harmful phenomenon? If no, what is its importance?
written.finalAnswer: Transpiration is a necessary evil. Although it is the loss of water from a plant, it creates a pull on the water columns in the xylem. This pull transports water and salts from roots to leaves.

written.text: Describe the events involved in the opening and closing of stomata.
written.finalAnswer: During daytime, guard cells take in potassium ions from surrounding cells by active transport. Their solute concentration increases, so water moves from epidermal cells into guard cells by osmosis. The guard cells become turgid; their inner sides move away from each other and the stoma opens. In the evening, glucose concentration falls and potassium ions move back to epidermal cells. Water moves out of the guard cells, they lose turgor, their inner sides touch and the stoma closes.

written.text: Describe temperature, wind and humidity as the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
written.finalAnswer: An increase in temperature increases the rate of transpiration because water evaporates more quickly at higher temperature. explain.title: What transpiration means
explain.body: The loss of water in the form of vapours from plant surface is called transpiration. Water can leave through stomata in leaves, the cuticle on the leaf epidermis, or lenticels in the stems of some plants.

explain.title: How water vapour leaves a leaf
explain.body: Water moves from xylem into the cell walls of mesophyll cells. It evaporates from the moist walls into the leaf’s air spaces, then moves towards the stomata and passes into the outside air. Most transpiration occurs through stomata and is called stomatal transpiration.

explain.title: How stomata open and close
explain.body: Stomata open and close because the turgor pressure of their guard cells changes. In daytime, potassium ions enter guard cells by active transport; water follows by osmosis, making the guard cells turgid and opening the stoma. In the evening, potassium ions move back to epidermal cells and water leaves, so the guard cells lose turgor and the stoma closes.

explain.title: Why transpiration matters and what affects it
explain.body: Transpiration is a necessary evil: it creates a pull on water columns in the xylem, helping transport water and salts from roots to leaves. Higher temperature and wind increase transpiration, while higher humidity lowers it. Leaves with more surface area transpire more, and in most plants the lower leaf surface transpires more because it has more stomata.

mistakes: Do not say that guard cells open because water leaves them; water enters them by osmosis during daytime, making them turgid.
Do not reverse the evening events: potassium ions and water move out of guard cells, and the stoma closes.
Do not write that humidity increases transpiration; higher humidity lowers its rate.
Do not give only the effect of temperature or wind: include the reason given in the section.
Do not confuse transpiration with only stomatal water loss; water can also leave through the cuticle and lenticels.
